questions.q: Why does the lesson say a public model leaderboard doesn't answer the question most builders actually have?
options: Leaderboards measure general capability on broad benchmarks, which says little about performance on your specific prompts, data, and task
Leaderboards are always inaccurate and should be ignored entirely
Leaderboards only cover models released before 2020
Leaderboards are a paid feature not available to most developers
questions.explain: The lesson explains that general leaderboard scores don't reflect how a model performs on your specific workload.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend as the way to actually compare candidate models for your use case?
options: Picking whichever model has the most social media buzz
Running your own eval dataset and grading criteria against each candidate model, so the comparison is apples to apples
Always choosing the newest model regardless of performance
Relying solely on a single public benchmark score
questions.explain: The lesson recommends running the same eval dataset (from Lesson 7) and grading criteria (from Lesson 8) against each candidate model.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why did one model fail a test case even though its answer content was correct?
options: It used the wrong programming language
It exceeded a latency threshold, which was graded as a separate assertion from content correctness
It refused to answer the question at all
It was not included in the eval dataset
questions.explain: The lesson's example shows a model passing on content but failing a latency assertion, illustrating that failures can be unrelated to answer quality.

questions.q: Besides quality/pass rate, what other factors does the lesson say belong in a model comparison?
options: The model company's stock price
Cost per request/token and latency, at the volume and interactivity the application actually requires
The number of employees at the AI company
The color scheme of the provider's website
questions.explain: The lesson lists cost and latency, at real expected volume, as essential comparison axes alongside quality.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say reading a per-case assertion breakdown matters more than just an aggregate score?
options: Because aggregate scores are always wrong
Because an aggregate score tells you a model is worse but not in what specific way, which per-case detail reveals
Because per-case detail is required by law
Because aggregate scores take longer to compute than per-case detail
questions.explain: The lesson explains that per-assertion detail separates 'wrong content' from 'right content but a different failure,' which an aggregate score alone can't show.
